notes: Sample reports_config.json - which reports are built, how often, and how stale a measurement may be before it stops counting. Copy to reports_config.json and edit.

Two levels of scheduling, on purpose. data/app_commands.json decides how often the reports APP wakes up; this file decides which report is due when it does. Adding a report therefore never means touching the scheduler.

'metric_max_age_seconds' is the freshness gate: a metric older than this is not reported at all. Without it a report quietly restates yesterday's numbers as though they were current, which is worse than reporting nothing - so an hourly report keeps a short window and a daily summary a long one.

'time_window' is the same shared scheduling object the daemon and the SQL tasks use. from_hour/to_hour confine a report to office hours; 'repeat_interval' is seconds and is counted from the previous run's start.

'report_base_url' is the public address the rendered pages are served at - it appears in delivered messages as the link back to the full report. Leave it empty when nothing serves the pages; the reports are still written to runtime/reports.

'inventory_exclude_ip_prefixes' hides address ranges from the inventory pages. It was a constant inside the rendering library until it became clear that the library was deciding which of an estate's machines nobody gets to see. Empty means show everything.

reports._note: The morning digest: everything measured in the last day, whatever its severity. A day of tolerance is right here because the report IS the daily picture.
Fifteen minutes of tolerance, because a warning about a measurement taken an hour ago is a statement about the past. The short window is what makes this report actionable.
A week of tolerance, deliberately. A database backed up weekly still has a valid, week-old measurement, and a freshness gate of one day would report it as unmonitored rather than as backed up.
